name: Zac Robinson

views.text: A great quarterback's preparation raises the whole staff's level of detail.
You borrow from the coach who trained you, but you cannot copy him; you build your own version.
Formation looks are tools; if defenses think they have you figured out, show them something else from the same look.
A slow opener usually starts with the play-caller, and the fix is cleaner execution and fewer giveaways.
Have the two-minute calls ready before you need them, so a late drive is just the plan running.
A young quarterback benefits from hearing it straight from his coordinator, face to face on the sideline.
Outside criticism of a scheme is often a convenient story; the tape says what really went wrong.

signatures: credits the quarterback and the line by name after a good drive, and takes the blame himself after a bad one
explains a scheme choice by listing the variations it hides rather than defending the label
refers back to what he learned beside McVay and Stafford in Los Angeles
want: to show that a McVay-tree quarterbacks coach can run his own offense and grow a young passer in Atlanta
fear: that his offense gets labeled predictable and the young quarterback's struggles get pinned on him
voice: Calm, polite and analytical, a former quarterback who talks in the language of coverages and packaging. He spreads credit to players and owns slow starts, but pushes back firmly when he thinks a criticism of his scheme is lazy. Rarely raises his voice in public.

evidence.summary: Morris says Robinson's lack of play-calling experience does not concern him and he trusts him fully; reports that about six teams pursued Robinson before he chose Atlanta. Local item, Morris's view.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Rams On SI), Anthony Licciardi
evidence.summary: Robinson credits McVay with starting his coaching career, describes him as transparent and accessible, singles out his pregame preparation and plan structure, and says he will use those lessons rather than try to be a copy. His own words.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Falcons On SI), Jon Alfano
evidence.summary: At his introduction he calls Stafford the smartest player he has been around, a meticulous preparer who forced coaches to match his detail; they remain close friends. Notes his rise from assistant to Rams QB coach and pass game coordinator. His view of one player.

In his second game calling plays he scripts a late winning drive at Philadelphia, having readied two-minute calls in advance; he credits execution, the line and Cousins, and says the Week 1 problems started with him. Reporter describes him as calm and self-critical.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Falcons On SI), Scott Kennedy
evidence.summary: An analyst attacks the heavy pistol usage as predictable and limiting for Penix; Robinson answers that the pistol is versatile, the run game uses many snap points, and the team adapts to defenses, calling the critique a convenient narrative. Criticism plus his rebuttal.

He moves from the booth to the sideline for the first time; Penix says direct feedback built confidence, Bijan Robinson says he explained coverages, and the offense posts season highs. He is not quoted directly; a teammate relays that he said he should always have been downstairs.
